subject: dragonling
reasoning:
I'm planning out a TypeScript module that builds a baby dragon model using the SDK, mapping out the joint, chain, and builder APIs I'll need to use correctly for a compact but well-shaped rig.

Sketching joint placements for a baby dragon roughly 1.2m long, facing +Z: hips as the root joint near the base of the spine, then a spine chain running up through chest to shoulders, built via a catmull path with named segments for easy reference later.

I'm working through how parent resolution flows in the chain-building logic — the catmull path's first vertex needs to connect back to the hips joint explicitly so the spine chain starts rigidly attached rather than snapping to whatever joint happens to be nearest.

Thinking about it more, I'm leaning toward using sprout for the limbs (neck, legs, wings, tail) since it conveniently builds a chain starting from an existing joint's frame, auto-naming segments based on the path's knot spans. For legs specifically I'll pass an explicit catmull or bent polyline path into sprout rather than relying on defaults, so the bend is controlled precisely.

For a leg with hip, knee, ankle, and toe points, I'd pass four names so the first three map to joints at each knot and the last maps to the tip, matching the spans+1 naming rule. Rather than fighting sprout's auto-prefix logic, I think it's simpler to just pass the full point list directly as the path, trusting that the starting point matches the body joint closely enough to avoid triggering the prefix check.

I'm reasoning through how sprout resolves its starting frame — it reads the joint's world position as the root, and the given path's first point needs to match that within tolerance, which should hold since matrixWorld uses float64 precision throughout. The new joint's parent weighting ties back correctly to the body joint, and sweep will operate over the chain's span joints as expected; now I need to work out how the radius function should vary across the swept limb.

For the limb taper I'm picking a radius array like [0.09, 0.07, 0.05, 0.035] interpolated smoothly over the parameter. I'm also confirming sweep will rigidly bind to the single parent joint when there's no chain source, and that it extends the start of the sweep backward along the tangent based on the max radius there.

For the torso itself, I'm weighing whether to use sweep with a radius profile versus loft with explicit stations (position, width, height) along the spine — loft seems more convenient for a body shape, though I need to check how its bone weighting resolves since there's no owner chain, meaning it'll likely bind rigidly to the nearest single joint along the path.

To let the torso bend more naturally rather than being rigid to one joint, sweeping along the spine chain itself makes more sense so the body smoothly blends across the spine joints, with the radius function returning separate width and height values per ring, oriented relative to the chain's tangent, normal, and binormal frames depending on how the "up" vector is defined for that chain.

I'm reconsidering the spine joint setup, thinking it might be cleaner to skip chains for the body and instead define explicit joints—hips, chest, neck base, head—placed along a curved path with named spans so the sweep follows the spine's natural shape from root to chest.

I'll just accept the redundancy and name the root joint "pelvis," since chains need a root joint to attach to and this works fine despite the near-duplicate position. Now I'm working out the torso sweep shape along the spine chain, varying the radius with a sine-based function to get a stylized belly curve from hips to chest.

For the head, I'm considering whether to use a sweep/loft off its own small joint or just place a sphere-like part — leaning toward a stylized loft with stations positioned in head-local coordinates, attached to a head bone.

Defining head loft stations...

Now I'm working on the jaw: a separate joint hinging near the back of the mouth, parented to the head, with a rod-shaped sweep running forward toward the mouth tip with a slight taper in radius.

Jaw joint inherits parent orientation without its own aim, so it follows the head joint's quaternion. For the head-neck chain, I'm figuring out how the spine's chain joints map onto path knots—spine1, spine2, and chest sit at parameter positions along the catmull path, with the chest joint ending the spine chain so the neck chain can attach there and continue up toward the head.

Now I'm sketching out proportions for a baby dragon: big head, short legs, folded wings, and a tail, working through spine coordinates to get the body's curvature and radius right so the back height and belly line make sense.

For the legs, I'm figuring out where hips and shoulders attach so the toes land close to ground level with a small allowed sink, then planning hip and shoulder joints parented to the pelvis root so each leg can sprout from the correct frame.

Actually, I realize I should avoid creating a separate hip joint and instead have the leg sprout directly from a point on the spine chain, letting the span joint parent it naturally. The catch is that the spine's position at an arbitrary parameter isn't a known fixed constant since it's a curve through control points, so I need another way to get that exact coordinate for the sprout's starting point.

I'm now leaning toward a cleaner approach: using b.chain for each leg with explicit joint names (hip, knee, ankle, toe), parenting the chain's root to the pelvis directly rather than trying to splice into the spine curve.

With the leg represented as a polyline through hip-knee-ankle-toe points, the chain's spans will give proper orientation frames at each joint, and the sweep can follow this path with tapered radii to round out the leg shape at the corners.

I want the leg to taper from thick at the hip to thin at the toe, so I'm using a radius function of t rather than a fixed array, since the knots aren't evenly spaced along the polyline. For the foot, I'm weighing whether to treat the toe as just the chain's endpoint with a small radius, or build a separate capsule-shaped foot piece attached at the ankle, leaning toward keeping it simple by letting the leg chain itself terminate at the toe near the ground with a thin radius there.

Now I'm adding small claws at each toe using spike sweeps pointing forward-and-down, checking that sweep/spike functions accept a color option so I can paint them dark. I'm also planning the overall coloring approach using a shared paint texture sheet for countershading, spots, and scales across all body meshes rather than flat per-mesh colors.

For the palette, I'm settling on emerald green with a cream underbelly, orange-red spines and horns in cream, pink-ish wing membranes, and yellow eyes with black pupils. I'm working out how to combine paint functions—using countershade layered over a spotted pattern for the body so the back has mottled green spots fading into the cream belly.

Now I'm thinking through the wing structure itself: a shoulder-to-wrist arm chain, finger chains branching out to tips, and membrane fills stretched between the finger edges and the body side to create that classic bat-wing look.

I'm placing the wings with shoulder-elbow-wrist chains extended outward and upward for a spread rest pose, naming the joints shoulderL/elbowL/wristL with the shoulder parented to the chest bone. Then I'm setting up the finger chains branching from each wrist joint, making sure each chain's root inherits parentage correctly from the wrist bone.

For the wing membranes, I'm defining the leading and trailing edges connecting adjacent finger chains together, plus a body-edge polyline running from the wrist back down toward the flank and hip to close off the membrane shape.

Now I'm sketching out finger tip positions relative to the wrist, fanning them out from a leading front finger to a rearward one so the membrane spreads naturally across the wing.

I'm working out the body edge polyline from the rear finger's tip down toward the hip, and thinking through how the membrane should parameterize across columns between adjacent fingers and into the body edge so the arc-length alignment stays consistent.

Membranes can accept either a chain or a plain point path, so passing the wrist-based array works fine; I'll give them a thin pink fill color and keep it simple rather than building a gradient. I'm setting up a mirrored builder function so left and right wings share geometry but flip across x, with left as positive sign, then I'll extend this to a tail chain running back from the pelvis through the hips.

Now I'm plotting the tail's path points, tapering its radius from a thicker base near the pelvis down to a narrow tip, and adding a spade-shaped slab at the very end for visual flair.

For horns, I'll use spikes from base to tip points attached to the head joint directly, avoiding ambiguous nearest-joint attachment since that could accidentally bind to the jaw instead. For the back spines, I'm thinking of computing positions manually along the spine chain using frame data rather than relying on built-in helpers, since I need precise control over the outward-and-up direction at each point.

Working out approximate body-top heights at several z positions along the spine, then placing small embedded spike bases with upward-and-back tip directions so they look naturally mounted into the body surface.

Now I'm working out the spike directions and attaching them loosely to the nearest spine bone, then moving on to the hind leg joint chain—placing hip, knee, ankle, and toe positions for a bent sitting stance and tapering the thigh radius along its length.

Next I'm defining the front leg joints (shoulder, elbow, wrist, toe) with a backward-bending elbow and forward-reaching foot, then separating out the wing arm's shoulder root position on the upper back distinct from the front leg shoulder.

I rename joints to avoid collisions: front legs use "shoulderL/elbowL/wristL/pawL" while wings use "wingRootL/wingElbowL/wingWristL", both parented to the chest joint near the top of the spine chain. Now I'm working out the neck chain's starting point from the front of the body.

Then I sketch the head's loft stations from back of skull through cheek, eye zone, muzzle, to the snout tip, figuring sizes and z-positions so the neck joins cleanly into the back of the head, and I define the neck chain's three segments connecting into that head joint.

Actually simpler: I'll make the head joint separate via b.joint with explicit parent, aim, and role, while the neck chain stops at three named joints ending right at the head's position so the sweeps connect cleanly. For the neck sweep itself I'm tapering the radius slightly toward the head and need to check that the start cap doesn't overlap awkwardly with the body.

For the head I'm using a loft over a small set of stations built from catmull-interpolated points, letting the radius function return matched x/y values since the head is roughly round, and tagging the loft with the head bone so it deforms correctly with the skeleton.

For eyes, I'm planning to use a surface query against the head loft to find the nearest point and normal, then stick small sphere geometries there so they sit flush on the curved head surface rather than floating at an arbitrary offset.

That protrusion of 0.056 is a bit much for a googly eye, so I'm considering a smaller radius like 0.03 for the eye sphere itself. For the pupil, I'm working out how to position a small black sphere on the front face of the eye, computing its offset along the normal from the eye center so it sits correctly stuck to the eye's surface.

I'll also add tiny dark nostril spheres embedded at the snout, and sketch out brow horns as small spikes rising from the top of the head with a slight backward tilt.

Now I'm working out the jaw structure — placing a hinge joint near the back of the head and running a rod forward to form the lower jaw, positioning it just beneath the head's lower surface so it reads as a distinct jawline rather than merging into the skull.

I'm giving the jaw a cream color to match a typical dragon's belly/underside tone, then turning to the forelegs with clawed toe spikes and sketching out the wing structure — chains of finger joints spreading from the wrist to the tips, each sweep tapering outward to form the membrane supports.

I'm defining membrane meshes stretched between pairs of finger chains and between the outer finger and body edge, using lerped points between the two boundary paths at each parameter t, with a scallop factor that pulls the trailing edge inward to create a natural curved wing silhouette.

For the right wing, I mirror everything across the x-axis. For color, I'm setting up a countershaded body paint with greenish spots on the back and cream underside, reusing that same paint for the legs and considering whether the head and neck should share it too.

Defining the module export...

I'm checking ground contact at each foot and toe joint, adjusting radii and y-coordinates so nothing clips below the floor — nudging the toe height to 0.03 to keep a safe margin, and verifying claw spikes stay clear of the ground too. I'm now working out the hind leg joint positions (hip, knee, ankle, toe) to get a natural stance.

I'm laying out the front leg chain from shoulder to toe, making sure the elbow bends backward naturally and the toe points forward, then checking that the body's belly clearance above the ground looks right given the leg lengths. I'm also placing the wing root on the back near the chest joint and starting the wing arm chain from root to elbow to wrist, and now moving on to defining the tail joint chain.

Setting up tail joints and spade...

Adding orange spikes along the spine, then building the head surface so I can sample nearest points on it for placing the eyes with proper bone weighting.

For the eye stick placement, I'm computing how deep to embed the sphere so the eye sits slightly proud of the head surface rather than sunken in — settling on an embed value around 0.33 to get roughly 0.02 protrusion with a 0.03 radius sphere. Now I'm adding the pupil as a smaller sphere positioned relative to the eye center.

I'm tweaking the pupil's offset along the surface normal so it protrudes just enough past the eye surface to be visibly distinct (around 0.009 sticking out) rather than sitting flush or buried.

I'm confirming the hit normal and eye center calculations use the surface's axis getter correctly, and that the pupil is rigidly weighted to the head bone. Now I'm moving on to placing the nostrils using a similar nearest-surface-point lookup.

I'm also checking whether the horn bases, placed near the back of the head loft, actually sit within the head's cross-section radius -- they're slightly outside the ellipse boundary but the horn's own base radius should cover that gap. I'm deciding to skip cheek frills and brow ridges for now, color the horns with the HORN material, and tint the wing membrane fingers orange, keeping the overall design moderate rather than overloaded.

Setting up the import for the geometry classes needed...

Defining the color palette and body shading function...

Now I'm setting up the skeletal rig, starting with a pelvis joint as the root and building a spine chain that runs through the pelvis, lower spine segments, and chest, checking that the path and parenting types line up correctly before moving on to the body mesh sweep.

For the torso, I'm building a sweep along the spine chain using a radius function shaped by a bulge curve, making sure the tuple return type is explicit so it matches the sweep's radius signature, then starting a neck chain running from the chest up through several neck joints toward the head.

Now I'm defining the head joint parented to the neck's last segment with an aim vector pointing slightly forward and up, then starting a loft for the skull using a series of width/height profile points tracing from the base of the head up to the crown.

Checking the loft station radii and spacing against the neck's endpoint to make sure the back of the skull fits cleanly over the neck connection. I'm noticing the jaw tip sits too close to or inside the head's bottom radius at that z-position, so the jaw ends up partially hidden rather than hanging visibly below the skull. I need to reposition the hinge point lower and adjust the tip coordinates so the jaw clears the head's underside properly.

For the slight-open pose, I'm working out which rotation direction about the jaw's local X-axis moves the forward tip downward versus upward — using the standard rotation formula for Y/Z components, a positive angle about X pushes the forward-pointing Z component toward negative Y, which reads as the tip dropping down, so that's the direction I want for opening the mouth.

Good, confirming the mesh stays parented to the joint so posing the jaw works correctly. Now I'm setting up the eye placement logic, finding the nearest surface points on the skull for left and right eyes, sticking spherical eyeballs there embedded into the head, and positioning small pupil spheres offset along the surface normal.

Still writing nostril placement...

Now I'm adding horns using the spike helper with base and tip points for each side, then setting up spine spikes along the back by computing y-coordinates as a function of z position for each spike's base location.

I'm building the tail chain with five joints running from the pelvis back toward the tip, then sweeping a tapering radius profile along it for the tail mesh, and defining the spade shape at the tip using a flat polygon with Newell normal calculation.

Writing the mirrored limb-building function now, using a helper to flip x-coordinates for left/right symmetry across hind legs, fore legs, wings, fingers, and membranes...

Defining the remaining finger paths and wing membrane geometry...

Placing claws forward along each toe, offsetting their base position so they sit near the toe tip and angle slightly downward, with three per foot spaced across the width and colored to match horn material, keeping the geometry tucked within the toe's radius so they don't float free.

Still checking the API signatures for membrane, part, stick, pose, surface, and joint creation to make sure parent/root logic and role tags work correctly for the pelvis and head joints.

I'm verifying chain point counts against span and name requirements for spine, neck, tail, legs, wings, and fingers, plus confirming the jaw joint parent and polyline knot distribution match the expected path geometry.

Now I'm drafting the full dragon skeleton and mesh code: joints for pelvis, spine chain, head, jaw, and symmetric loops for hind legs, front legs, wings with finger chains and membranes, tail, and eye/claw placements, mirroring left/right sides with a helper function. I'm working through parent-child joint ordering, role tags, naming collisions, and tuple typing for coordinates and colors, while double-checking that chains, sweeps, spikes, rods, and membranes all take valid PointInput/JointRef arguments rather than raw strings where objects are required. I'm also verifying paint colors (scales, horn, wing membrane pink, eye glow), triangle/part counts stay reasonable, and that the final return of the builder root is correct before assembling everything into one complete TypeScript code block.
